newsitem.title: USA: Unlikely coalition attacks U.S.-China trade policy.
newsitem.headline: Unlikely coalition attacks U.S.-China trade policy.

text.p: A coalition of unlikely allies including Christian, labour, human rights and some business groups on Wednesday attacked President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's privileged trading status.
Although the critics conceded it would be hard to rally enough support in Congress to overturn Clinton's decision, they signalled a major battle in the coming weeks.

Clinton said on Monday he would accord China most favoured nation status for the coming year despite disagreements over human rights and other issues as he pursued a policy of engagement with Beijing.

Coalition members, stating their case at a news conference, included such disparate forces as the Family Research Council, an ultra-conservative organisation known for its opposition to abortion, the Campaign for Tibet, labour unions, and liberal and conservative members of Congress.

California Representative Nancy Pelosi, a long-time China foe, said: "By following a policy which bolsters the Chinese government, the United States is actually supporting the containment of the Chinese people, their hopes and aspirations."

Virginia Republican Representative Frank Wolf said religious repression, the treatment of dissidents, alleged slave labour in prison camps and the U.S. trade deficit with China combined to increase congressional scepticism about the Clinton policy.
"I believe there is going to be a sea change in the Congress," Wolf said, although he acknowledged it would be a struggle to get enough votes to override a presidential veto.

Coalition members said the United States' $40 billion trade deficit with China last year could exceed $50 billion this year. Only a handful of "elite exporters" benefited from dealings with China, they said.
U.S. trade figures released on Wednesday showed a continuing trade gap with China but the monthly deficit narrowed by 22.4 percent in March to $2.59 billion from $3.34 billion in February.

"We are told that trade and capitalism bring democracy to China. Nothing could be further from the truth of historical reality," said Jeffrey Fiedler, president of the Food and Allied Service Trades Dept., affiliated with the AFL-CIO.

John Carr, an official with the U.S. Catholic Conference, said: "MFN may not be the perfect vehicle but is our nation's best chance to insist we will no longer ignore religious persecution, violation of worker and human rights, and coercive abortion policies."
Some members of Congress have already said they will seek to reverse Clinton's move to renew China's MFN status, an annual decision that every president has made since 1980.

Under the law, Clinton must formally inform Congress of his decision by June 3. The House of Representatives and the Senate, to overturn the decision, have until Aug. 31 to pass a joint resolution disapproving it.
If Clinton were to veto such a resolution, both chambers would then have to muster a two-thirds majority to override his veto and prevail in the annual policy battle.
The debate was sharpened this year by rising concern about the handover of the British colony Hong Kong to China on July 1 and reports of Chinese weapons proliferation.
Investigations into alleged Chinese attempts to influence U.S. political campaigns in 1996 were also likely to make the debate even more divisive.
Chinese human rights activist Harry Wu, speaking in a Senate hearing discussing reports of Chinese forced labour, added his voice to the opposition.
"I know the Chinese didn't deserve our favour" when MFN was renewed earlier in the Clinton administration, he told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee "They still do not deserve our favour."
Wu, an exiled former detainee who heads a foundation monitoring forced labour in China, said he believed there were up to eight million prisoners in Chinese forced labour camps.
